summary: Defines distributed mobility anchoring, the configurations and functions for IP mobility where multiple anchors let a session switch mid-session. It applies to network-based and host-based mobility.

eli5.summary: Instead of one big station everyone must go through while moving, many small stations share the job.

questions: how does ip mobility use multiple anchors
why is routing inefficient with a single anchor
how does a mobile node choose between address continuity and efficiency
subtitle: Multiple IP anchors let a mobile device maintain connections when switching networks

tldr.problem: As mobile devices move between networks, they face a choice: change their IP address (breaking ongoing connections) or keep it (requiring inefficient routing through a distant anchor point).
tldr.mechanism: Distributed Mobility Anchoring (DMM) uses multiple anchor points in the network so a device's traffic can be anchored near its current attachment point. Different flows can independently choose whether to maintain address continuity or switch to a new address.
tldr.outcome: Applications can select, per flow, whether they need IP mobility (address continuity) or can tolerate an IP address change. This enables both efficient routes and flexible session handling.

today: RFC 8818 is an Informational RFC that describes distributed mobility anchoring as a research-oriented framework. It complements earlier IETF work on distributed mobility management and serves as a reference for network operators designing systems where mobile devices maintain connections across network boundaries. Various standardized protocols like Proxy Mobile IPv6 and Mobile IPv6 can be deployed within this DMM framework.

sections.title: The Mobile IP Problem
sections.content:
Traditional mobile IP systems use a single home agent that anchors a mobile device's IP address. When the device moves to a new network, all its traffic must still route through the distant home agent, even though the device is now closer to different network equipment. This creates inefficient, long-distance paths and puts all mobility load on a single point.

Distributed Mobility Anchoring solves this by having multiple anchors in the network. Each anchor can host IP addresses for mobile devices, and when a device attaches to a new network, it can optionally use an address anchored at that new location. This keeps traffic paths short and distributes the mobility load.
sections.eli5: Instead of one big post office everyone goes to, every neighborhood has its own post office that can handle mail.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The architecture separates control-plane functions (location management and policy decisions) from data-plane functions (actually forwarding packets). Anchoring means an anchor node advertises a route into the network for a particular IP prefix, ensuring all traffic for that address flows through the anchor.

Two key functions manage this: the Location Management (LM) function tracks where a mobile node is attached and maintains bindings between IP addresses and their current locations. The Forwarding Management (FM) function actually forwards packets to the correct destination based on this location information. A Home Data-Plane Anchor (H-DPA) is topologically anchored for the mobile node's IP address, while an Access Data-Plane Anchor (A-DPA) is where the mobile node is currently attached.
sections.eli5: The control plane is the decision-maker (where is this person now?), and the data plane is the delivery system (forward this letter there). Different anchors handle different devices, keeping paths short.

sections.title: Two Deployment Models
sections.content:
Network-Based DMM handles all mobility functions within the network infrastructure. Mobile nodes do not need to run any special software; the network manages location tracking and forwarding on their behalf. The network can have a centralized control plane that coordinates multiple distributed data-plane anchors, or both can be distributed. This approach works well when the network operator wants to manage mobility transparently.

Client-Based DMM puts some responsibility on the mobile node itself. The mobile node performs its own forwarding management and location management, typically by maintaining multiple IP addresses and choosing which one to use for each flow. A network location manager still tracks where the mobile node is, but the device has more control over how it handles mobility. This approach is more flexible but requires sophisticated client software.
sections.eli5: Network-based means the post office handles everything automatically. Client-based means the person decides which address to use and tells the post office where they are.

sections.title: Choosing When to Keep Your Address
sections.content:
DMM defines three cases for handling IP addresses when a mobile node moves. In the nomadic case, the application does not need the IP address to stay the same. When the device moves, it simply gets a new IP address from the new network and uses it for new connections. The old address becomes unusable, so this approach works only for applications that can tolerate connection interruption.

In the mobility case with traffic redirection, the device keeps its original IP address anchored at the original network, but when it moves, the original anchor forwards traffic to the device's new location (typically using IP tunneling). New connections can use the new network's address if desired. This balances address continuity with reasonably efficient routing.

In the mobility case with anchor relocation, the IP address anchoring itself moves to the new network. This requires more sophisticated mechanisms to redirect traffic but keeps routes optimized. Applications needing strict address continuity but optimal routing would use this approach.
sections.eli5: Nomadic: get a new address in the new place. Redirection: old address still works but bounces through the original office. Relocation: the address moves with you.

sections.title: How Mobility Works in Practice
sections.content:
When a mobile node attaches to an access router, it receives a Router Advertisement containing an IP prefix for that network. The node configures an IP address from this prefix. If the node later moves to a different access router, it receives a different prefix and can configure a new IP address.

For flows that do not need address continuity, this is straightforward: the application closes the old flow and starts a new one with the new IP address. Routing works normally since the address belongs to the new network.

For flows that need address continuity, the original anchor must continue to route traffic toward the mobile node. If the anchor receives a packet destined for the mobile node's old address, it must forward it to the new location. The mobile node may establish a tunnel back to the original anchor for reverse traffic, or the network may use other indirection mechanisms. Higher-layer protocols like MPTCP or QUIC can also assist by allowing connections to migrate between IP addresses.
sections.eli5: Arriving at a new address: the network tells you your new address. No continuity needed: switch addresses and reconnect. Continuity needed: the old address still delivers mail by forwarding it to you, or you tunnel back to get mail from the old address.

layers.detail: The device moving between networks, maintaining one or more IP addresses

layers.label: Control Plane (Location Management)
layers.detail: Tracks where the mobile node is and manages address bindings

layers.detail: Routes packets to/from the mobile node based on location information
